1.26.m: Bhīṣma said: / A man would be endowed with long life, health, great increase of lineage, and possessed of beauty and good family, / birth after birth; tell me fully the observance of the cool-rayed [moon] by which [he becomes so].
Pulastya said: / This was properly asked by you, [an observance] producing imperishable heaven; / I will declare the secret that knowers of the Purāṇas know.
Here the observance named the couch-sleep of Rohiṇī and the Moon is spoken of; / therein one should worship the image of Nārāyaṇa with names of the Moon.
Whenever the bright fifteenth day happens to fall on a Monday, / or Rohiṇī coincides with a full-moon day,
then a man should bathe with the five products of the cow and mustard seeds; / and the learned person should repeat one hundred and eight times [the verse], 'Swell up' (āpyāyasva).

Even a śūdra, with supreme devotion, avoiding talk with heretics: / 'Homage to Soma, the peaceful one,' the two feet; 'Homage to the endless abode,' the knees and shanks; / 'To the water-bellied one,' the two thighs; and one should worship the penis saying, 'To the abode of the bodiless one [Kāma].'

'Homage, homage to the giver of amorous delight,' the hips of the moon should always be worshipped; / likewise the belly, 'To the ambrosia-bellied one'; the navel should be worshipped with 'Homage to the hare-marked [moon].'

'Homage to the moon,' the face; constantly the teeth are to be worshipped with 'To the lord of the twice-born'; / the smile is to be worshipped with 'Homage to the moon'; the two lips, 'To the one who loves the forest of white water-lilies.'
And the nose, 'To the lord of the excellent herbs'; again, the two eyebrows, 'To the seed of joy'; / the pair of eyes resembling a lotus, likewise, 'To the moon'; the blue water-lily […] of Śauri;

'Homage to the one worshipped in all sacrifices,' the two ears; 'To the slayer of the Daityas'; / the forehead of the moon, 'To the lover of the ocean'; the hair of the lord of the Suṣumnā is to be worshipped.

The head, 'Homage to the hare-marked [moon]'; 'To Murāri, the lord of the universe,' then 'Homage,' the diadem; / 'To the ocean of nectar of fortune and happiness named Lakṣmī and Rohiṇī, who is dear to the lotus.'

Having worshipped the goddess, the wife of the moon, with fragrant flowers, / food-offerings, incenses, and the like, / the one who, having slept on the ground and risen again, has bathed, eats sacrificial food, and to a brāhmaṇa
a water-jar with gold should be given in the morning, saying, 'Homage to the destroyer of sins.' / Having consumed cow's urine, meatless food, and non-pungent food, twenty-eight

morsels, and three morsels mixed with ghee, having fasted and eaten, he should listen to legendary history for a muhūrta: / kadamba, blue lotuses, ketaka, / jātī, white lotuses, and hundred-petaled roses,
amlāna flowers, then sinduvāra, and again the flower of the Bhārata mallikā, / white flower, oleander flower, and auspicious campaka are to be offered to the moon,
in order, in the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, at all times. / In whatever month the observance begins, one should worship Hari with its flowers.
Having fasted thus for a year in accordance with the rule, a man, / at the end of the observance, should give a bed furnished with bedding accoutrements.
Having had a pair of Rohiṇī and the Moon made of gold— / the Moon should be made six fingers [high], Rohiṇī four fingers [high]—
furnished with eight pearls and provided with white eyes, / and placed upon a milk-jar with a bronze vessel filled with unbroken grains,
he should give it in the forenoon with the mantra, accompanied by rice, sugarcane, and fruit, / along with a white cow with a golden face and silver hooves,
with a cloth and a vessel, and likewise a conch and a vessel. / Having adorned a virtuous brāhmaṇa couple with ornaments,
one should imagine: 'This moon is in the form of a brāhmaṇa, along with his wife. / Just as Rohiṇī does not ever leave your bed, O Kṛṣṇa,
so also for you who have the form of the Moon, there is no difference from me through your manifestations. / Just as you alone are the giver of liberation and supreme bliss to all,
so let there be enjoyment, liberation, and firm devotion to you, O Moon, for me.' / Thus, for one terrified of saṃsāra and desiring liberation, O sinless one,
this bestower of beauty, health, and long life is unexcelled; / and this alone is always dear to the ancestors, O king.
Having become the lord of the three worlds for three hundred and seven kalpas, / he attains the world of the moon, from which return is hard to obtain.
Or whatever woman performs the couch-sleep of Rohiṇī and the Moon, / she too attains that fruit, from which return is hard to obtain.

He who recites or hears thus the worship of the Slayer of Madhu along with the praise of the Moon, / and even gives his mind [to it], goes to the abode of Śauri and is worshipped by the hosts of immortals.

1.27.m: Bhīṣma said: / For ponds, pleasure-groves, wells, step-wells, and lotus pools, / and for shrines of the deities, tell me the rite, O brāhmaṇa.
Who are the officiating brāhmaṇa priests there? What kind should the altar be? / The priestly fee, the offerings, the time, the place, and the master priest?
What substances are praised? Declare it all, O you of good vows! / Pulastya said: / Hear, O long-armed king, the rule that applies to ponds and the like.
This legendary history is recited in the Purāṇas, O best of kings: / Having reached the auspicious bright fortnight, and when the northern course of the sun has arrived,
on an auspicious day declared by brāhmaṇas, having performed the blessing recitation of brāhmaṇas, / in a place free from inauspicious things, near the pond,
an even, four-cornered altar, four cubits [in size] with four openings; / likewise the pavilion should be sixteen cubits [in size] and four-faced.
Around the altar, pits measuring an aratni, with three tiers, / nine, seven, or five, with straight openings, O prince.
The yoni [receptacle] should measure a span, six or seven fingers broad, / and the pits should measure a cubit, with tiers raised three finger-breadths.
On all sides they should be of matching color, furnished with pennants and banners. / Made from branches of the holy fig, cluster fig, waved-leaf fig, and banyan,
one should have these doors made in each direction of the pavilion. / Auspicious eight hotṛs [should be] there, and likewise eight gatekeepers;
eight repeaters of prayers should be appointed, brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, / complete in all marks, knowing mantras, with senses conquered,
endowed with noble family and character; one should indeed install these best of twice-born; / at each pit jars and implements of sacrifice.
A fan, a bright seat, and a broad copper vessel [are prepared]; / then there should be offerings of varied colors for each deity.
The wise priest, having consecrated [them] with mantras, should scatter [them] upon the earth. / A sacrificial post should measure one cubit, made from a milky-sapped tree,
or equal to the height of the sacrificer, erected by one who desires prosperity. / Twenty-five officiating priests, adorned with gold ornaments, are to be appointed:
earrings of gold, upper-arm bands, and bracelets, / as well as sacred darbha rings for the fingers and various garments.
He should give equal [shares] to all; for the chief priest, it is taught to be double. / He should also give a bed, along with whatever is dear to himself.
Two golden [images]: a tortoise and a makara; two silver: a fish and a water-snake; / two copper: a crocodile and a frog; an iron crow and a gangetic dolphin.
Having procured all of that at the very beginning, O ruler of the people, / wearing white garlands and white garments, anointed with white fragrant unguents,
bathed with waters of all medicinal herbs by priests who have crossed to the far shore of the Vedas, / the sacrificer, accompanied by his wife and accompanied by sons and grandsons,
having reached the western entrance, should enter the sacrificial pavilion. / Then, with auspicious sounds and with the beating of kettle-drums,
one who knows the truth should make a mandala with five-colored powder: / then a sixteen-spoked wheel, four-faced, with a lotus in the center,
four-cornered all around, and circular and very beautiful in the middle. / Having made [it] upon the altar, then the planets and the guardians of the worlds
the wise one should deposit according to the mantras in every direction. / In the middle he should set up a water jar, accompanied by a mantra to Varuṇa.
There the wise man should establish Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu; / and having installed Vināyaka, Kamalā, and Ambikā,
he should then place the hosts of beings for the pacification of all worlds. / Having thus performed the preliminary consecration with flowers, edible offerings, and fruits,
he should wrap those jars, which have jewels inside them, with cloths. / Having adorned the guardians of the doorways on every side with flowers and perfumes,
he should say to them, “Sacrifice!” and he should honor the chief priest. / Having stationed two Ṛgvedic priests in the east, and two knowers of the Yajurveda in the south,
two Sāmavedic singers are to be stationed in the west, and two Atharvavedic priests in the north. / Facing north, the sacrificer should sit to the south.
He should speak once more to those sacrificers: “Sacrifice!” / and to the reciters: “Remain engaged in the recitation of the supreme mantra!”
Having thus instructed them all and rekindled the fire, the knower of mantras / should offer oblations with mantras: clarified butter and firewood.
The officiating priests too should offer oblations with mantras to Varuṇa on all sides. / Having offered according to rule to the planets, and likewise to Indra and Īśvara,
to the Maruts, to the guardians of the world, and according to rule to Viśvakarman, / the Ṛgvedic priest in the east should recite the Śāntisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānasūkta,

and the auspicious Puruṣasūkta separately. / Those knowers of the Yajurveda in the south should recite the hymn to Indra, the hymn to Rudra, the hymn to Soma, / the Kauṣmāṇḍa hymn, the Jātavedas hymn,
and the hymn to the Sun. / The Sāmavedic singers, O king, stationed at the western entrance,
should sing the Vairāja, the Puruṣasūkta, the Sauparṇa, the Rudrasaṃhitā, / the Śaiśava, the Pañcanidhana, the Gāyatra, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, / the Vāmadevya, the Bṛhatsāman, the Raurava, the Rathaṃtara,
the Gavāṃ Vrata, the Vikīrṇa, the Rakṣoghna, and the Yāma hymns.
And the Atharvavedic priests in the north, relying in their minds upon the lord, the god Varuṇa, / should recite the pacifying and prosperity-bestowing hymns.

Having thus performed the preliminary consecration through the night on the preceding day, / having taken earth from [a track of] elephants, horses, and chariots, an anthill, a confluence [of rivers], and a cow-pen,
he should throw it into the water jars, and likewise medicinal herbs, / yellow orpiment, white mustard, perfumes, and bdellium.
The ritual bathing of the patron is to be performed first, accompanied by the five products of the cow, / with great mantras, having done so according to rule.
Having spent the night in this manner with the ritual action prescribed by rule, / then at clear dawn, when it has broken, a hundred cows
should be given to the Brahmins, or sixty-eight, / or fifty, or thirty-six, or twenty-five.
Then, when the moment arrives at an auspicious and pure astrological ascendant, / accompanied by Vedic chanting, gandharva music, and various musical instruments,
having adorned a cow with gold, he should lead her down into the water; / and she is to be given to a Sāmavedic Brahmin, O ruler of the people.
Taking a golden vessel provided with the five gems, / and then placing therein makaras, fishes, and so on of all kinds,
borne by four Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / filled with water from a great river, adorned with curd and unhusked barley,
he should make it overturned, facing north, in the midst of the water. / Bathed well with an Atharvan hymn, and likewise [with] the Māyā hymn,
having cast [the vessel] with the mantra “āpo hi ṣṭha”, and returning to the pavilion, / having worshipped the members of the assembly, he should distribute offerings on every side.
Again offerings are to be made for four days, O best of kings; / the Fourth-Day Rite is to be performed, and gifts given there according to one's capacity.
Having prepared the sacrificial vessels and the sacrificial implements, / he should distribute them equally to the priests, and then divide the pavilion.
He should present a golden dish and a bed to the Brahmin. / Then a thousand Brahmins, or eight hundred,
or fifty, or twenty, should be fed according to capacity. / Thus is the procedure for a reservoir proclaimed in the Purāṇas.
For all wells, stepped wells, and lotus-ponds, / this very procedure is ordained, and likewise in consecrations [of them].
There may be variation according to mantras in the case of temples and garden grounds. / But for one who is incapable, half of this procedure is ordained by the Self-born.
In minor rites, it is to be performed as with a single fire by those free from dishonesty regarding wealth. / Water that remains during the rainy season is considered equal to an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
that which remains in the autumn yields the fruit spoken [for that season]; / that which remains in early winter and late winter [is equal] to the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices.
They declare that water which remains during the spring season is equal to a horse sacrifice; / water that remains even in the summer surpasses the Rājasūya.
The person of exceedingly pure intellect who performs these special dharmas on earth, O great king, / goes, purified, to the abode of Brahmā, and rejoices in heaven for many kalpas.
Roaming across numerous worlds such as Svar, and enjoying [pleasures] with celestial women for two parārdhas, / by the power of that yoga he ultimately attains the supreme state of Viṣṇu.

1.28.m: Bhīṣma said: / Tell in detail, O Brahmin, the rule for trees as it truly is, / according to which rule the planting of trees should be performed by the wise,
and which worlds are taught for them—tell me those now. / Pulastya said: / I will declare the rule for trees and likewise for garden grounds.
Having completed everything like the procedure for a reservoir, O lord of the earth, / with the priests, the pavilion, the materials, and an ācārya of the same kind,
he should honor the Brahmins likewise with gold, garments, and unguents, / sprinkled with the waters of all medicinal herbs, adorned with curd and unhusked barley.
Having adorned the trees with garlands, one should wrap them with garments; / with a golden needle, the piercing of the ears should be performed for all of them.
Collyrium should likewise be applied with a golden rod, / and one should cause seven or eight fruits to be made of gold.
One should consecrate them on an altar for each of all the trees; / the best incense here is bdellium placed in copper vessels.
Having placed pots filled with seven kinds of grain, / with garments, fragrances, and unguents, at all the trees, O lord of the earth,
and having worshiped them at the end of the day, making offerings of oblations / duly to the world-guardians beginning with Indra, according to the rule,
in this manner the preliminary consecration of the lord of the forest should be performed by the twice-born. / Then, [wearing] white garments and wearing a golden girdle,
from the midst of the trees one should release a milch-cow facing north, / accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, highly resplendent with two golden horns.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments and auspicious songs, / and with the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāma mantras, and those dedicated to Varuṇa, all around at that time,
the eminent brāhmaṇas should perform the ablution with those very pots. / Bathed and wearing white garments, the sacrificer should worship
all the concentrated priests with cows according to his wealth, / with golden threads, bracelets, rings, and purification cords,
with garments, beds, and likewise household implements and sandals; / and he should sprinkle them with milk for four days.
A fire sacrifice should be performed with clarified butter, barley, and black sesame seeds; / palāśa kindling sticks are recommended, and likewise a festival on the fourth day.
And the sacrificial fee should again be given there according to one's capacity in the same way; / free from envy, he should give whatever is dearest [to him].
Having given twice as much to the preceptor, he should bow down and beg forgiveness. / The wise person who performs the tree-festival according to this rule
attains all desires and reaches the endless abode. / And the wise person who even thus establishes a tree, O king of kings,
he too would dwell in heaven, O king, for thirty thousand periods of Indra; / he redeems past and future human beings, equal in number to [his body] hairs.
He attains the highest accomplishment, from which return is rare. / The person who regularly hears this or recites it to others
is also worshiped by the gods and honored in the world of Brahmā. / Even trees grant sonship to a childless man;
they offer the balls of rice and other funeral rites at holy pilgrimage sites to their planters. / Even with effort, O king of kings, plant an aśvattha tree;
it alone will accomplish the duty of a thousand sons for you. / One becomes wealthy through an aśvattha tree; the aśoka destroys grief;
the plakṣa is said to bestow sacrifices, and the kṣīrī is remembered to bestow long life; / the jaṃbū gives a maiden daughter, and likewise the pomegranate bestows a wife.
The aśvattha is for the destruction of illness, and the palāśa bestows Brahman; / a state of being a ghost arises for the man who plants a vibhītaka.
In the aṅkola is the increase of family, and through the khadira is freedom from disease; / the sun is ever pleased with those who plant the nimba.
Lord Śaṅkara [dwells] in the bilva tree; Pārvatī in the pāṭalā; / apsarases in the śiṃśapā; the best of gandharvas in the kunda;
hosts of servants in the tamarind, and likewise dāsyus in the vañjula; / the sandalwood and the jackfruit bestow merit and prosperity;
the campaka bestows fortune, and the karīra leads to adultery; / the palmyra palm destroys offspring; the bakula increases the family;
the coconut tree brings many wives; the grapevine brings one charming in all limbs; / likewise the jujube bestows sexual pleasure; the ketakī destroys enemies.
Such trees, and other ones that have been mentioned, are bestowers [of fruits]; / those by whom trees have been planted will attain firm establishment.

1.29.m: Pulastya said: / 'Likewise I shall declare another [observance] that yields the fruit of all desires, / named Saubhāgyaśayana, which the knowers of the Purāṇas know.'
Formerly, when the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahaḥ were burnt, / the fortune of all beings then became united in one place.
Reaching Vaikuṇṭha, it all settled on Viṣṇu's chest. / Then, after some time, during the arrangement of the new creation, O king,
when the world was enclosed by ego and joined with primal matter and the spirit, / and when rivalry increased between the lotus-seated Brahmā and Kṛṣṇa,
a terrible flame of fire of tawny form arose. / From Hari's chest, heated by it, that [fortune] issued forth
which, taking shelter on the chest of Viṣṇu, had rested as fortune. / As it took the form of liquid, before it reached the surface of the earth,
it was intercepted from the atmosphere and merely drunk by the wise son of Brahmā, / Dakṣa, producing beauty and charm;
great strength and splendor arose for Dakṣa, the Parameṣṭhin. / That remainder which fell upon the earth was produced in eight forms.
From that arose seven fortune-bestowing plants: / sugarcane, the king of trees, the niṣpāva bean, and the śāli rice-grain;
and cow's milk with its modifications, safflower, and flowers; / and salt is the eighth; likewise it is called the eightfold fortune.
What was drunk formerly by the son of Brahmā, the knower of yoga and knowledge, / became his daughter from that [essence], she who is named Satī.
Because of surpassing the worlds in loveliness, she is called Lalitā; / the wielder of the Pināka married the goddess, the beauty of the three worlds.
Full of the fortune of the three worlds, bestowing the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, / having propitiated her with devotion, what does a man or woman not attain?
Bhīṣma said: / 'How is her worship [performed], O sage, the worship of Lalitā? Tell me! / And what is the ritual procedure for the pacification of the world? Tell me that!'
Pulastya said: / 'Upon reaching the spring month, on the third lunar day, loved by the people, / in the bright fortnight, in the forenoon, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds.'
On that day, they say, that goddess, the fair-complexioned Satī, / was married to the universal soul with the mantras of hand-taking.
Then, together with her, on the third lunar day, one should worship the lord of the universe / with various kinds of fruits, lamps, incenses, accompanied by food offerings.
Having bathed the image with the five cow-products and likewise with fragrant water, / one should worship Gaurī accompanied by the moon-crested [Śiva].
Saying: 'Obeisance to Pāṭalā', the two feet of the goddess and of Śiva; / reciting: 'To Śiva', and 'To Jayā', at the two ankles;
saying: 'To Tryambaka', the pair of shanks for Rudra, and 'To Bhavānī' [for the goddess]; / saying: 'To the lord Śirorudra', and 'To Vijayā', the two knees;
reciting: 'To Harikeśa', and likewise 'To the bestower of boons, obeisance', the thighs; / saying: 'To Īśa', the waist, and 'To Śaṅkara', for Śaṅkara, [and] to Rati [for the goddess];
the two sides of the abdomen to Koṭavī, and the wielder of the trident to Śūlapāṇi; / saying: 'To Maṅgalā, obeisance to you', one should worship the belly;
'To the soul of all, obeisance', for Rudra, and the two breasts to Īśānī; / in the same way, Śiva to the embodiment of the Veda, and the neck to Rudrāṇī one should worship;
to the destroyer of Tripura, the lord of the universe; the pair of hands to Anantā; / to the three-eyed Hara, the two arms; [and the goddess's arms] to the beloved of the fire of cosmic dissolution;
saying: 'To the abode of good fortune', one should always worship the ornaments; / saying: 'To Svāhā and Svadhā', the face, and to Īśvara, the trident-bearer;

the two lips, which bestow prosperity, are to be worshiped as belonging to the dweller in the Aśoka grove; / likewise, the face to Sthāṇu, to Hara, [and to the goddess] 'To the beloved of the moon-faced one'.
"Homage to Hara, half woman, the lord!" [one should worship] the nose with "O Asitāṅgī!"; / "Homage to the fierce one, the lord of the world!" [one should worship] the two brows with "O Lalitā!"
[One should worship the teeth] for Śarva, the destroyer of the city; the locks of hair likewise with "O Vāsudevī!"; / and "Homage to Śrīkaṇṭhanātha!"—thus one should worship the hair of Śiva.
"To the one of formidable, fierce, and terrible form!"; "Homage to the soul of all!" for the head. / Having duly worshipped Hara, [one should place] before him the eight auspicious gifts:
one should set out smooth beans, safflower, milk, cumin, / sugarcane—the king of plants—salt, and coriander as the eighth.
One should give it because it bestows good fortune; hence it is called the eight auspicious gifts. / Having thus offered all that before the two auspicious deities, then
in Caitra, having eaten water chestnuts, one should sleep on the ground, O subduer of foes. / Then again in the morning, having bathed and chanted prayers, pure,
having worshipped a twice-born couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments, / [one should present] two golden images accompanied by the eight auspicious gifts:
"May Lalitā be pleased with me!"—one should offer [these] to a brāhmaṇa. / In this way for a full year on every third day, O king.
Learn from me this distinction regarding the food to be eaten and the mantras of donation: / In Madhu, water from a cow's horn is prescribed; in Vaiśākha, cow dung;
in Jyeṣṭha, a mandāra flower; a bilva leaf is prescribed in Śuci; / in Śrāvaṇa, curds should be eaten; but in Nabhasya, water with kuśa grass;
milk in the month of Āśvayuja; in Kārttika, clarified butter with curds; / in Mārgaśīrṣa, cow's urine; in Pauṣa, one should consume ghee;
likewise in Māgha, black sesame seeds; and the five products of a cow in Phālguna. / Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, Śivā,
Vāsudevī, and Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī, / and Umā: at the time of giving, one should declare: "May she be pleased!"
In that twelfth month, on the twelfth lunar day, one should worship Kṛṣṇa; / likewise, one should worship Lakṣmī there together with her husband.
Therefore, on the full-moon day, the grandfather together with his wife / should likewise be worshipped by the wise person who desires freedom from fear in the next world.
Similarly, the eight auspicious gifts must be given by one who desires prosperity: / jasmine, aśoka, lotus, kadamba, blue lotus, campaka,
kubjaka, oleander, bāṇa, amlāna, red lotus, / and sinduvāra are declared to be the flowers in all the months.
Hibiscus, safflower blossoms, mālatī, and the hundred-petaled rose, / as available, are praised, and oleander is suitable at all times.
Having thus fasted duly for a year, a man, / a woman, or an unmarried girl, having worshipped Śiva with devotion at night,
at the conclusion of the vow should give a bed furnished with all utensils, / golden Umā and Maheśvara, and a bull together with a cow.
Having set them on the bed, one should present it to a brāhmaṇa. / Having worshipped Keśava with Mahālakṣmī on the twelfth lunar day for one year,
and Brahmā with Sāvitrī, a man in this world / obtains all desires cherished in his heart.
Other couples also [he should honour] according to his ability with garments and the like, / with gifts of grain, ornaments, cows, and other accumulations of wealth.
Free from deceit regarding wealth, without pride, he should worship them. / Whoever properly performs the vow of the bed of fortune in this way,
attains all desires, or enjoys an eternal abode. / While performing this, he should undertake the abandonment of one fruit [each month].
He attains renown and fame each month, O ruler of men; / endowed with good fortune, health, beauty, clothes, ornaments, and decorations,
he will not be separated [from them], O king—the giver of the bed of fortune. / He who performs the vow of the bed of fortune for twelve years,
or for seven or eight, is exalted in the world of Brahmā. / Being worshipped, the man resides properly as long as ten thousand kalpas.
Then, having reached the world of Viṣṇu, he goes likewise to the world of Śiva. / The woman or unmarried girl who performs it, O lord of men,
she too obtains that fruit, cherished by the goddess's grace. / Whoever listens to it or even gives encouragement,
he too becomes a Vidyādhara and resides in the heavenly world for a long time. / This was instituted here formerly by Madana, and likewise performed by Śatadhanu as a man;
and it was performed by Pavana and by Nandin—why then, O ruler of people, should it not be a great wonder?

1.30.m: Bhīṣma said: / "Having reached the Yajñaparvata mountain, why were footprints given / here by the all-powerful Viṣṇu? For what purpose was the path of footprints
made by the god of gods? Tell me that, O noble-minded one. / Which Dānava was subdued here by that Viṣṇu
after placing his footsteps? Tell me that, O great sage. / Viṣṇu's residence is in the heavenly world, in the Vaikuṇṭha of that great soul.
How did he set down his feet in the mortal realm? / Indeed, in the heavenly worlds, the gods, preceded by Indra,
are constantly devoted to the Lord through great asceticism, O brāhmaṇa. / The residence of glorious Varāha is celebrated in Maharloka;
that of the great-souled Nṛsiṃha is declared to be in Janaloka; / the residence of Trivikrama is celebrated in Tapoloka.
Leaving these worlds, how did he place his two feet on the earth, / and in this sacred site of the Grandfather, at Puṣkara on Yajñaparvata?
Relate to me at length, O brāhmaṇa, how he made his footprints. / By hearing this, the destruction of all sin will surely come about."
Pulastya said: / "You ask well, sir! Listen attentively to that: / how formerly the placement of footprints was made by the god Viṣṇu,
having reached Yajñaparvata, on the slope of the rocky mountain. / Long ago, in the Kṛta age, O Bhīṣma, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose,
it was done formerly by Viṣṇu for the sake of the earth, O tormentor of enemies. / The entire heaven was brought under control by the mightier Dānavas,
having subdued the three worlds and defeated the gods, along with Indra. / The Dānavas were the eaters of sacrifices there, being more powerful;
they were all led by Bāṣkali, the mightier Dānava. / When the three worlds, both moving and unmoving, were in such a state,
Śakra fell into supreme distress and became despairing of his life: / 'This Bāṣkali, the lord of Dānavas, cannot be slain by me in battle
due to the boon given by Brahmā to him, nor by all the gods. / Therefore, I, surrounded by all the gods, in the world of Brahmā,
go for refuge to the god; no other recourse exists.' / Having reflected thus, the lord of gods, accompanied by all the denizens of heaven,
went swiftly, O Bhīṣma, to where the divine grandfather was. / Reaching the abode of Brahmā and surrounded by those gods,
he spoke of the matter concerning the world and of the utmost distress that had arrived: / 'O god, do you not know the reason why fear has come to us?
Since everything has been seized by the Daityas through your boon, O Lord, / all about the wicked Bāṣkali has indeed been told by me.
Let action be taken without delay; you are our father and grandfather. / Consider the truth, O lord of gods, for the pacification of the world here!
While they look on, no rites of the Vedas or traditions proceed at all; / our destruction increases day by day through them.
Just as an ordinary person speaks with an aim toward his own self-interest, / so you are addressed by us, who are continually deprived of help.'
If a foolish-minded person does not act in return for the benefit rendered by another, / increased a thousandfold, that person's mind is in vain.
For that shameless, wicked person, burnt by unrequited favor, / a dwelling place in hell is assured for committing such evil.
Goodness does not consist merely in doing a counter-service for a deed done; / yet even this does not arise in those whose minds are devoted solely to self-interest.
If any place of this world has not become painful, / its torn heart in a hundred pieces has not reached satisfaction.
Deliver us who are submerged therein or wherever we might go, / by stating a means through which [our] splendor may prevail.
Look upon the world situated as I have described and seen: / devoid of Vedic recitation and the vaṣaṭ call, its festivals and auspicious celebrations ceased,
abandoned by connection with study, devoid of engagement in trade and agriculture, / forsaken by the science of governance, and reduced to breath alone.
The world has attained affliction and a state even more miserable; / during this time, we have arrived at exhaustion."
Brahmā said: / "I know that Bāṣkali, arrogant on account of the grant of a boon, / is invincible to you; I think he will be subdued by Viṣṇu."
Then Brahmā, having restrained himself, remained fixed in essential reality; / from the mere contemplation of him absorbed in concentration, the four-armed [Lord appeared].
Being meditated upon by the Self-born in a very short time, / he arrived within an instant, right before the eyes of all.
Viṣṇu said: / "O Brahmā, turn back from this meditation, you are released from it; / for whatever purpose this meditation is desired, that I have come to you."
Brahmā said: / "This great favor here is indeed the vision of the Master. / To whom else, O Lord, could this concern for the world belong?
My very origin was fashioned for the sake of the world; / this world is meant for you; in truth, there is no wonder [in this].
Protection is to be performed by you, while Rudra alone would destroy. / When this world has become such, from this high-souled Indra,
the kingdom—the three worlds with the moving and unmoving—was seized by Bāṣkali. / Let assistance be given to your servant by granting counsel, O Keśava."
Vāsudeva said: / "By your granting of a boon, he is now incapable of being slain; / that Dānava must indeed be conquered by intelligence, through bondage here.
I shall become Vāmana, the destroyer of the Dānavas. / Let this [Indra] go with me to the dwelling of Bāṣkali.
Having gone there, let him beg this boon for my sake: / 'O King, grant three paces of land to this brahmin dwarf,
"Bestow [it], O highly fortunate one; this request was made by me." / Spoken to by Śakra, the lord of the Dānavas would give even his own life.
Having received a gift from that Dānava, O grandfather, / and then having bound him with effort, making him a dweller in the underworld,
having assumed the form of a boar, I shall exist for the destruction of that evil-minded one; / of this there is no doubt. Go, O Indra, endowed with haste."
Having spoken thus to him, he ceased and indeed disappeared. / Then, after a period of time, when Viṣṇu entered the womb of Aditi,
exceedingly dreadful portents appeared in great numbers; / yet, when Viṣṇu, the support of the entire universe, entered the womb,
auspicious and mighty omens also arose at that time: / a sweet, fragrant breeze carrying the perfume of mālatī blossoms blew.

Then, having reached the appointed time, the God, who has compassion on all beings, / with pure sparse hair, bearing the splendor of the rising moon and conch, for the welfare of the hosts of gods, the God of gods assumed the state of Aditi's son.

And when Viṣṇu descended, the faces of the Siddhas, gods, and asuras, whose eyes were unblinking, became exceedingly bright; / with winds blowing with dust utterly subsided, the day of Viṣṇu's birth from the auspicious womb came to be.

That divine Aditi, having conceived, proceeding slowly, afflicted by the heavy burden of her rounded hips, lovely in her gentle gait, / bearing the fatigue of a weary face and paleness, carrying the very heavy, deep womb—
then, when Nārāyaṇa indeed entered the dwelling of the womb, through the conjunction of past and future, / all beings then became free from misfortune, their desires attained.
The wind blew very gently, while showers of flowers fell upon mountain peaks, / the pathways in all directions became clear, and the people indeed attained truth.
As the sky was freed from dust and darkness slowly vanished, / while Viṣṇu was within the belly, an intention of hostility arose [in her]:
"Listen to that, O best of kings, as it occurred to the mother of the gods in order: / 'Shall I leap across heaven without any gradual order?
I will make that Bāṣkali, the lord of Dānavas, a dweller in the underworld! / For wealth and beauty were given by me to Indra.
I alone am capable of destroying the Dānavas! / I cast multitudes of arrows and numerous discus-chariots,
and various hosts of maces for the destruction of the Dānavas! / The wise gods shall dwell in heaven, and the Dānavas below the earth;
I shall do this through the agency of time, for that duty is my vow!' / Such speech suddenly came forth, abiding in her mouth.
[Then she thought:] 'By whom has this been contemplated before, which was neither seen nor heard? / Look at my bondage of the chief of Danu's sons, wrought in anger!
Wealth and beauty were formerly given to Kaśyapa. / Why is this [mind] devoid of enthusiasm, or why are the winds agitated?
My vision as it were reels; this form was not imagined by me. / Am I possessed, that I speak an improper word with someone?'
Falling under the power of doubt, she repeatedly reflected in her heart; / she bore the divine Lord for a thousand celestial years.
Then there was born from her Vāmana, the dwarf of beings, / by whose birth the eyes of the Dānavas were indeed stolen away.
As soon as that god of gods, Janārdana, was born, / the rivers flowed with clear waters, and a fragrant wind blew.
Kaśyapa also attained joy through that radiant son; / the enthusiasm of mind of all those dwelling within the three worlds [was aroused].
Then, as soon as Janārdana was born, O ruler of the people, / kettledrums sounded in heaven, struck by them.
Out of the supreme delight of the three worlds, delusion and sorrows went to destruction; / and the host of Gandharvas sang exceedingly, mingled with emotional notes directed to their master.
And the celestial women, groups of Apsarases endowed with emotion, danced there; / likewise, crowds of Vidyādharas and Siddhas, rejoicing, roamed about in aerial vehicles.
They spoke determining what was true and untrue in actions, and displayed dramatic performances; / their passions subsided, they sang songs again and again, abounding in pain and pleasure.

And those who had gone to heaven danced, departing from here to heaven earned by righteousness; / thus, in the purified living world freed from sorrow, released from the mass of darkness, they were eager to attain bliss.

There some said on the earth, “Victory, victory to the Lord!” and some were overjoyed; / thus indeed, with unbroken concentration, through uttered shouts and others' repetitions, / others meditated in secret upon the cause that severs the fear of birth, old age, and death; thus this entire world was rejoiced on all sides.
Approaching this supreme Viṣṇu, Brahmā said for the sake of the world: / “Although he is the Lord, he is born for your sake as Vāmana.
He is Brahmā and Viṣṇu, he alone is Maheśvara; / he is the Vedas and the sacrifices, and he is heaven, without doubt.
All this world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded by Viṣṇu; / being one, he is known as Svayambhū through distinct manifestations.
Just as a crystal gem appears diverse depending on its colored backing, / so too is the course of that self-existent one according to the influence of the guṇas.
For just as the Gārhapatya fire attains other names, / so indeed does that Lord receive names among Brahmā and the others.
In every way, the divine Vāmana will accomplish the mission of the gods.” / While those gods, whose minds were composed, were thus reflecting,
he went together with Indra to the dwelling of Bāṣkali. / And seeing from afar his city surrounded
by white, chief mansions adorned with all kinds of jewels, unreachable by birds, / with well-divided royal highways,
graced by hundreds of rutting elephants resembling Mount Añjana, / born of the breed of divine elephants,
adorned with slender-bodied horses with small ears, swift as thought, / having long necks and lovely eyes,
and with thousands of courtesans there, radiant as gold from the lotus-womb, / whose faces resembled the full moon, skilled in conversation and playful banter,
there was no merit, no branch of learning, no craft, no art / that was not present in Bāṣkali's city, turning toward a dwelling there.
Crowded with hundreds of gardens, garlanded with gatherings and festivals, / populated by chief Danus, all free from death,
everywhere resounded with the sounds of vīṇās, flutes, and mṛdaṅgas, / the Danujas ever delighted, adorned with many jewels,
were seen sporting just like the immortals on Mount Meru. / A great roar of Vedic chanting was uttered there by the elder Danus,
its sins cleansed by the wind carrying the ghee-smoke of the sacrificial fires, / its air perfumed by the scattering of fragrant incense,
in that city crowded with fragrant Danujas, / having subdued the three worlds, the Dānava Bāṣkali lived in comfort.
Staying there, he ruled the three worlds, both moving and unmoving, / knowing dharma, grateful, truthful, and having conquered his senses,
pleasant to look upon for the primeval gods, discerning in policy and impolicy, / pious toward brāhmaṇas, a refuge, and compassionate toward the wretched,
whose energy was augmented by Vedic mantras, endowed with all powers, / zealous in the field of the sixfold foreign policy, speaking always with a smile,
knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, an offerer of sacrifices, devoted to austerity, / never inclined toward bad conduct, non-injurious everywhere,
honoring the venerable, pure, pleasant-faced, worshiping the worshipful, / knowing all matters, unassailable, fortunate, and handsome to behold,
having abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many vehicles, the Dānava / was an achiever of the three aims of life, ever the best of men in the three worlds.
Ever dwelling in his own city, destroying the pride of gods and Dānavas, / he thus protected all the subjects in the three worlds.
While that Dānava was king, there was no vile person at all, / nor any wretched, sick, short-lived, or suffering one,
nor anyone foolish, dull-looking, unfortunate, or cast out. / Seeing him endowed with such pure abundance of virtues and perceiving his resolute intellect,
magnanimous Purandara, pleasing the best of Daityas, that foremost Danu, / that Dānava endowed with splendor, blazing like the sun,
capable of upholding the three worlds, was then astonished. / Seeing Indra arrived at the city, O king,
the Dānavas, intoxicated with battle, went and said this to the lord of Dānavas: / “Regard it as a marvel: Indra has come to your city,
alone, accompanied by a chief twice-born, a dwarf (Vāmana), O lord! / Tell us what we must undertake now, O sovereign ruler!”
He said to all the Dānavas: “Remain quiet in the city! / Let the king of gods be brought in; he is worthy of my worship today.”
At that very moment, Vāmana and Vāsava / arrived and were looked upon with love by the lord of Danus.
Considering himself fulfilled, the king, foremost among Dānavas, / having first bowed down, spoke these words:
“Today indeed, among the three worlds, there is none more blessed than I, / who, surrounded by prosperity, see Śakra arrived at my house.
Whatever he will ask of me, desirous of being a petitioner, / to him who has arrived at my house, I will surely give even my life;
what to speak of my wives, sons, house, or the three worlds?” / Coming face to face with him, respectfully taking him to his embrace,
embracing him, greeting him, he had him enter his house. / Having performed his welcome with arghya and other offerings, worshipping him with care, [he said]:
“Today my birth has borne fruit, all my desires are fulfilled, / since I see you, O Śakra, come in person to my home today.
By you I have been made renowned among the chiefs of Danus, O king of gods! / By coming to my home, supreme merit has indeed come to me.
Whatever fruit is obtained through the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices properly performed, / that fruit has been attained, O Purandara, upon seeing you.
Whatever fruit is attained by the gift of land, by the gift of cattle to the officiating priest, / or by the Rājasūya sacrifice, that fruit has become mine today.
The sight of you, O Vāsava, is not to be obtained by slight austerity. / Tell me what pleasing service is to be done by me in this house for you.
No other hesitation should be entertained in your heart in any way; / consider it done, even if it should be very difficult to accomplish.
I am meritorious, I have attained merit from the sight of you, O slayer of foes, / whose feet, praiseworthy by the best of gods, have been praised by me.
What is the purpose of your arrival? Tell me everything, O lord. / I consider the cause of your arrival to be an immense wonder.”
Indra said: / “I know you to be the foremost among the chiefs of Danus, O Bāṣkali; / upon seeing you, O best of Asuras, this does not seem a great wonder.
Suppliants who have come to your house do not go away empty-handed; / you are a wish-fulfilling tree to petitioners, and there is no other donor [like you].
In radiance you are equal to the sun, in depth like the ocean, / in forbearance like the earth, and in splendor like Nārāyaṇa.
This brāhmaṇa, Vāmana, was born in the auspicious lineage of Kaśyapa. / I was requested by him in this way: ‘Give me three paces of land
for my fire-sanctuary, where I may perform a sacrifice.’ / Making that his reason, this request of mine has arisen, O lord.
Having displayed prowess, the three worlds were seized from me by you, O Bāṣkali; / I am destitute of livelihood and penniless; whatever you might wish to give, that is not mine [to refuse].
I shall beg of you both for another's sake and for my own; / perform what is fitting for him and also for my state of being a petitioner.”
You were born in the lineage of Kaśyapa, an enhancer of your lineage; / born from the womb of Diti, your father is revered in the three worlds.
Knowing that you are such a person, therefore I make a request of you: / let three paces of land be given to him for the fire sanctuary.
To this dwarf of extremely small stature, O Dānava; / and in another's portion of land, I cannot venture to give.
This indeed is given by me, since you have been solicited by me, / if your elders or ministers approve of the three paces.
In accordance with my request, and with your own family and kin, / and when I have come to your house, act as is proper.
If it pleases you, O hero, O lord of the Dānavas of great splendour, / then let it quickly be given to this great-souled dwarf.
Bāṣkali said: / Welcome to you, O lord of the gods! Attain well-being without delay. / Look upon yourself, the refuge of all.
Having placed his burden upon you, the Grandfather sits at ease, / endowed with meditation and concentration, contemplating the supreme abode.
Wearied by many battles, having cast aside anxiety for the world, / Keśava sleeps happily, resorting to the island in the Milk Ocean.
And all the other mighty Dānavas equipped with weapons, / were all struck down by you alone without assistance, O Śakra.
The twelve Ādityas here, the eleven Rudras also, / the two Aśvins and the Vasus, and eternal Dharma—
resorting to the strength of your arms, they share in the sacrifices in heaven. / A hundred sacrifices were performed by you, completed with the best gifts.
And Vṛtra was slain by you, and Namuci, O Pākaśāsana; / previously by the mighty Viṣṇu who acted on your command,
Hiraṇyakaśipu's brother Hiraṇyākṣa was also slain; / and Hiraṇyakaśipu here was slain having been placed upon his lap.
Seeing you coming with thunderbolt in hand, seated upon the head of Airāvata / on the battlefield, all the Dānavas perish.
Those very powerful Dānavas who were conquered by you in the past— / I am in no way equal to a thousandth part of them.
You are such a one, O lord of the gods; what reckoning can there be of me? / With the desire to uplift me, your arrival was made indeed.
I shall do it, there is no doubt; I would even surely give my life. / For what reason, O king of the gods, was merely this land requested of me by you?
Here are wives, sons, cattle, and whatever other wealth exists; / let the entire kingdom of the three worlds be given to this brāhmaṇa.
Infamy would fall upon me and upon my ancestors, there is no doubt: / 'When Śakra came to his house, nothing was given by Bāṣkali.'
Whoever else comes to me as a petitioner is always very dear to me; / you especially in this case—do not entertain any doubt at all.
Great is my shame, O lord of the gods, that merely three paces of land / were requested by you for this brāhmaṇa in particular, O lord.
I shall give excellent villages to him, but heaven to you; / horses, elephants, land, wealth, and women with budding breasts,
by the mere sight of whom even an old man becomes young— / those women, and this earth, as a gift to the dwarf,
I shall give back, O lord of the gods; let favour be shown to me. / When these words were spoken by Bāṣkali then, O king,
the family priest Uśanas then addressed these words to the lord of the Dānavas: / 'You are the king, the lord of the Dānavas, established in eightfold sovereignty.
You do not know what is proper and improper, [or] what should be given by me to whom anywhere. / Having carefully deliberated with your ministers, and examined the proper and improper—
sovereignty over the three worlds was obtained by you having conquered the gods together with Indra. / At the end of these words of yours, you will certainly obtain bondage.
This dwarf who is here, O king, is none other than eternal Viṣṇu. / Nothing at all should be given to him by your majesty; your father himself was slain [by him].
This slayer of your father has arrived, the slayer of your mother, the destroyer of your kinsmen; / he has brought ruin to your lineage, and he will do so [again].
And he knows no righteousness; he is intent on the welfare of Śakra and the others. / He is a deceiver, by whom the Dānavas were conquered through deceit.
By deceit the form of a brāhmaṇa and a dwarf has been displayed. / What is the use of speaking much here? Nothing at all should be given to him!
If land measuring even the foot of a fly is given to him, / you will quickly go to destruction; truly, truly have I heard this.'
Addressed thus by his guru, he then spoke these words again: / 'Desiring righteousness, all this has been promised by me, O guru.
Fulfilling a promise must be done; it is the eternal duty of the virtuous. / If this is Lord Viṣṇu, there is no one more blessed than I.
Taking the gift from me, if he wishes to foster the gods, / then I have once more been brought to blessedness by this god, O guru!
He whose vision yogins endowed with meditation do not attain / even while meditating, and likewise the brāhmaṇas—he has been seen by me today!
Those who give gifts with hands accompanied by kuśa grass and water [say]: / 'May Lord Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Self, be pleased.'
When such a statement is uttered, one becomes a sharer in liberation. / As for this matter, how could hesitation arise in me regarding the performance of the act?
I was instructed by you, and in childhood I understood: / 'Even if an enemy comes to your house, nothing should be withheld.'
Reflecting on just this, O guru, I shall give even my own life / to the dwarf, and heaven to Śakra.
The gift which causes no affliction is the gift given here; / and the gift that causes affliction is remembered as a tainted gift.'
Hearing this, the guru stood there with downcast face in shame. / Bāṣkali said: / 'The request of your lordship [is granted], O god; all the earth should be given by me.
It causes me shame that there are only three paces of land for him.' / Indra said: / 'This is true, O lord of the Dānavas, what has been spoken by you to me.
A request for three paces of land was made to me by this twice-born. / By that much he is a petitioner, and I also on his behalf am [a petitioner] to you.
O son of Danu, you are solicited; let this boon be granted.' / Bāṣkali said: / 'Receive the three paces for the dwarf from me, O king of the gods;
dwell there happily for a very long time, O lord of the gods!' / Having spoken thus, the three paces were given to the dwarf by Bāṣkali,
poured out with water: 'May Hari himself be pleased with me.' / When it was given by the lord of the Dānavas, relinquishing his dwarfish form,
Hari strode across the worlds, desiring the welfare of the gods. / Having reached the Yajña mountain and having gone facing north,
the abode of the Dānavas was stepped upon by the god's left foot. / There the Lord of the World placed his first step upon the sun.
And the second upon Dhruva, O king; and with the third, / the cosmic egg was struck by that god of wondrous deeds.
When the egg was split by the tip of his big toe, abundant water rushed forth. / Having inundated the worlds of Brahmā, and all worlds in succession—
having inundated the station of Dhruva, the world of the sun, and that Yajña mountain, / that stream entered Puṣkara, having washed the feet of Viṣṇu.
Those footprints of Viṣṇu that were produced on the surface of the earth— / one who goes to that hermitage and bathes in the pool,
the fruit of a horse sacrifice arises for him by the mere sight [of them]; / accompanied by twenty-one generations, he attains residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
And having enjoyed immense pleasures for three hundred kalpas, / at the end thereof he is born as a universal monarch here on earth.
The formidable stream of water that issued from the tip of [Viṣṇu's] big toe, / that river is said to be Vaiṣṇavī, arisen from Viṣṇu's foot.
For this reason, O king, the Gaṅgā became Viṣṇupadī, / by which this entire triple world, with the moving and unmoving, is pervaded.
The auspicious water that entered from the universe's egg breached by the tip of his big toe, / that river which attained the status of the divine river is Viṣṇupadī.
By that divine river, O fortunate one, the cosmic egg with its moving and unmoving [beings] was pervaded / through her manifestations, out of a desire to show grace unto all.
That Bāṣkali was addressed by Vāmana: "Complete my steps!" / Then, with his face cast down, he found no reply.
Seeing him thus turned silent, the family priest said these words: / "The capacity to give is natural [to us], but we are not able to create.
As much earth as there is, O God, that much has been given to you by him, O Lord." / Bāṣkali said to Viṣṇu: "As much as the earth is—
which was created by you formerly—that has not been hidden away by me. / Small is the earth, and you are vast; I am not capable of creation.
Your power of will, O God, prevails always, O Lord." / Then Viṣṇu, considering him a speaker of truth, was left without an answer.
"Speak, O foremost of Dānavas: what desire of yours shall I grant? / The water placed in my hand has indeed been given by you, O Dānava.
Therefore you are worthy of a boon, an auspicious vessel for boons. / I shall grant your desire; ask for whatever you seek!"
Thus requested by him, the god of gods, Janārdana, [listened]: / "I choose devotion [to you], O Lord of gods, and death at your hand;
may I go to your Śvetadvīpa, which is difficult for [even] ascetics to attain." / When this was spoken, Viṣṇu said to him: "Remain right here for another yuga.
When, taking the form of a boar, I shall enter the surface of the earth, / then I shall slay you when you come before me."
Addressed thus by him, the Dānava retreated from his presence. / All the worlds were then traversed by Vāmana, O king.
Speaking the truth to the gods was then abandoned by those Asuras. / The Lord, the deity, having seized the three worlds, vanished from sight.
Dwelling in the netherworld, that Bāṣkali also lives happily, / and the wise Śakra protected the three worlds.
This is the manifestation named Trivikrama of the teacher of the universe, / accompanied by the origin of the Gaṅgā, destroying all sins.
This origin of the footsteps of Viṣṇu has been related to you, O king, / hearing which a man in this world is freed from all sins.
Nightmares, ill thoughts, hardships, and misdeeds / quickly go to destruction when the three footsteps of Viṣṇu are seen.
Seeing the sinful creatures through the succession of the yugas, / subtlety was shown by Viṣṇu, O Bhīṣma, in the sight of his steps.
A man on earth who climbs that [place] in silence, / having made the pilgrimage to the three Puṣkaras, would obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He is freed from all sins, and upon death he would go to Viṣṇu's city.

1.31.m: Bhīṣma said: / O venerable one, a great wonder indeed was the binding of Bāṣkali, / when Bali was restrained, the Trivikrama form having been assumed!
This was heard by me formerly as it was being narrated by the best of the twice-born, / [and that] Bali, the son of Virocana, lives in the netherworld even today.
How did the Nāgatīrtha come to be, and the origin of the Piśācas? / And how is Śivadūtī [here], and by whom was she rendered auspicious?
By whom was Puṣkara carried into the atmosphere, O great sage? / Tell me all of this, as also the binding of Bāṣkali.
The pacing of the earth was performed formerly by the god Viṣṇu; / what was the second cause for which the god did so?
Speak truly of all that in its reality, as it happened; / for this, which brings about the destruction of sins, should be heard by one desiring prosperity.
Pulastya said: / A burden of questions has been stated by you out of sheer curiosity, O king; / I shall tell you all of that as it happened, O best of kings.
In connection with the footsteps of Viṣṇu, the binding of Bāṣkali here / has all been heard by you, as it was proclaimed to you by me.
Again, O Bhīṣma, when the Vaivasvata interval arrived, / the three worlds were strode over by Bali, [and then] by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Going alone to the sacrifice, Bali was likewise restrained; / once again the pacing of the earth was performed by the god of gods.
The manifestation of Vāmana happened in that way, O lord of men: / having become Trivikrama, the dwarf became not a dwarf.
This entire origin has been related to you, O scion of the Kurus; / now listen to how the tīrtha of the serpents came to be, O you of great vows!
Ananta, Vāsuki, and the mighty Takṣaka, / Karkoṭaka the serpent king, Padma, and another reptile,
Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and the unconquered Kulika— / these are Kaśyapa's heirs, and by them the world was filled.
By their offspring this world was indeed filled— / crooked, doing terrible deeds, with sharp fangs, and swelling with poison.
Biting heedless men, they would turn them to ashes in an instant; / by their very sight the destruction of men would occur, O ruler of men.
Day after day, an exceedingly terrible destruction took place; / and seeing their own destruction, all creatures from all around
went for refuge to the refuge-giver, Brahmā, the supreme lord, / with this very matter in mind, all the creatures, O king.
Seeing the lotus-born ancient one called Brahman, they said: / The creatures said: / "O God, Lord of gods, source of the worlds, O supreme Lord!
Protect us from the powerful snakes of sharp fangs! / Day after day we see terror, O God, deeply miserable as we are.
Men, beasts, birds, and the rest—all of that turns to ashes! / The creation was made by you, O God, but it is being destroyed by the serpents.
Knowing this, do what is proper, O Grandfather!" / Brahmā said: / "I shall provide protection for you all, there is no doubt.
Go to your dwellings, free from sickness and rid of fear." / Thus all the creatures [were reassured] by Brahmā of manifest form.
Having praised the self-born one, they went away exceedingly pleased. / When the creatures had thus departed, summoning those serpents,
exceedingly enraged, he cursed them, with Vāsuki at their head: / Brahmā said: / "Day after day creatures are devoured by you vile souls;
bitten by snakes, men as well as beasts perish. / Because you constantly bring to destruction men who originate from me,
therefore, by my exceedingly terrible wrath, in another existence / let there be a terrible destruction of you in the future Vaivasvata interval!
Likewise another king, born of the Lunar lineage, Janamejaya, / will burn you in the blazed sacrificial fire with a snake sacrifice.
And Tārkṣya, the son of your mother's sister, will devour you. / Thus will be the destruction of all of you of wicked minds!"
Having cursed a thousand families so that only a single family remained, / when this was spoken by Brahmā, the foremost serpents, trembling,
falling at his feet, then spoke these words: / "O Lord, creator of all beings, crooked is our species;
excessive venomousness, cruelty, and the very nature of serpents / were brought about by you, O god; why do you curse us now?
Brahmā said: / If indeed you were created by me with crooked dispositions, / then why do you constantly devour [creatures] in large numbers, free of remorse?
The serpents said: / Establish an order, O Lord of gods, and separate realms [for each]; / make an agreement, O god, between men and ourselves.
By the curse which was given by you, the mortal Janamejaya / will cause our violent destruction through a snake-sacrifice.
Brahmā said: / There will be [a sage] renowned as Jaratkāru, foremost among knowers of the Veda; / a maiden of old age must be given to him, and a son will be born from her.
That brāhmaṇa, the purifier of your family, will protect you; / and I shall establish an agreement for the serpents along with human beings.
Therefore, all of you listen attentively to my command: / Sutala, Vitala, and thirdly Talātala—
these three kinds of dwellings have been granted to you; you shall go there. / Enjoying manifold pleasures there in accordance with my command,
dwell there repeatedly until the seventh age. / Then, at the beginning of the age of Vaivasvata, there will be a son of Kaśyapa,
an heir to all the gods, Suparṇa, the devourer of serpents. / Then the offspring of serpents will be burnt by the Fire-god.
And [this destiny] will certainly befall all of you; there is no doubt. / Those serpents who are cruel and undisciplined will meet their end; it cannot be otherwise.

Devour a creature when it is overtaken by its time, and a human being when harm has been done to you. / But toward mortals who are protected by mantras, herbs, the rites of Garuḍa, and protective charms,
you must act with fear, and harbor no other thought in your minds, or else destruction will come to you. / When this was spoken by Brahmā, all the serpents went to the realm named Sutala.
They all dwelt enjoying pleasures, staying at ease in Rasātala. / Having thus received both a curse and a favor from the Four-faced One,
they dwelt in their abode in the netherworld with gladdened hearts. / Then, after some time had passed, they again thought in this way:
“There will be a renowned king descended from Bharata, a descendant of Pāṇḍu, / who will cause our destruction through some decree of fate.
"How did the lord of the three worlds, the grandfather of all, / the creator of creation, adored by the world, place a curse upon us?"
Leaving aside the god Virañci, no other refuge is found; / that god resides in the excellent abode of Vairāja.
That god, abiding at Puṣkara, is currently performing a sacrifice; / having gone there, let us propitiate him; pleased, he will grant a boon.”
Thinking thus, all those serpents went to Puṣkara; / having reached the sacrificial mountain, they took shelter by the mountain ridge.
Seeing the serpents thus exhausted, streams of cool water, / flowing northward, emerged, bestowing delight upon all.
Thence arose the sacred site Nāgatīrtha on the earth, O bull among the Bharatas; / some call it Nāgakuṇḍa, and others call it a river.
It is sacred among all tīrthas, destroying the poison of serpents; / mortals who bathe there on the fifth lunar day of the bright half of Śrāvaṇa—
serpents will never cause affliction in their families. / The men on earth who perform an ancestral offering to the ancestors there,
Brahmā will grant them the supreme abode; there is no doubt in this. / Knowing the fear of the serpents, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
then recited to the serpents the words he had previously spoken. / That fifth lunar day is auspicious, destroying all sins and bringing welfare,
since on that very auspicious day the deliverance of the serpents was accomplished. / On this [tīrtha], whoever completely renounces pungent and sour foods,
and bathes the serpents with milk, achieves their friendship. / Bhīṣma said: / How Śivadūtī was born, and by whom she was installed—
all of that according to the truth you ought to tell me. / Pulastya said: / Śivānī reached the Blue Mountain, having resolved her mind on ascetic austerity;
she was the fierce power born from the matted hair [of Śiva]; hear her vow, O king: / “Having performed austerity for a long time, I shall devour the entire world!”
With this intention, that passionate woman practiced the five-fire penance. / Then, after some time had passed as the goddess performed that supreme austerity,
there was an asura of great splendor named Ruru, who had received a boon from Brahmā. / In the midst of the ocean is a very wealthy city named Ratnapura;
there dwelt that lord of the daityas, who struck terror into all the gods, / worshipped by many hundreds of thousands and hundreds of crores of foremost asuras,
the glorious one, like a second Namuci. / Then, after a long time, he went to the city of the world-guardians.
Desirous of victory, surrounded by an army, he chose enmity with the gods. / As that great asura rose up, the water of the ocean surged violently,
inhabited by many serpents, sea-monsters, and fish, flooding the slopes of the mountains; / containing within it numerous hosts of enemies of the gods, brilliant with varied armors and weapons,

a formidable army set in motion, with handsome warriors, emerged expansive from the waters of the ocean. / There elephants, mounted by daitya soldiers, equipped with bells and conveyances, and endowed with magnificence,
marched out, clearly displaying in their forms an equality with huge fish. / Likewise, horses bound with golden cords, like rohita fish at the water’s edge,

arrayed along with them, quickly marched out by hundreds of thousands and crores. / Likewise, chariots equal in speed to the chariot of the sun, fitted with wheels, staffs, axletrees, and bamboo poles,
their bodies secured upon mechanisms, with fluttering banners, made a loud roar. / And warriors standing on boats, desiring to cross, with excellent weapons in hand,
victorious in battle after battle, striking hard, shone brightly, following the asura in great numbers. / When the gods were in enmity and especially when they fled,
the asuras pursued all the gods in every direction. / Then all the hosts of gods, fleeing and overwhelmed with fear,
went to the excellent Blue Mountain where the goddess herself was staying, / the fierce, blessed, supreme power of Śambhu, endowed with austerity,
the goddess who brings about dissolution, whom they know as Kālarātrī. / Seeing the gods terrified and bewildered at that time,
the goddess with eyes like fully blossomed lotuses asked in wonder: / “Behind you I see no danger that has approached;
why have the gods, with Śakra at their head, all fled?” / The gods said: / “Here comes Ruru, the lord of the daityas, of terrifying prowess,
surrounded by a great fourfold army; / miserable because of him, we have sought you, O goddess, as our refuge.”
Hearing this speech of the gods, she laughed aloud; / as she laughed, fair-limbed women emerged from her mouth,
all holding nooses and goads, with plump, prominent breasts, / all bearing tridents, terrible, with fangs and hook-like faces,
all wearing diadems, biting their lips, / terrifying the moving and unmoving world with inauspicious hissing roars;
some wearing white garments, others wearing multicolored garments, / some with dark blue attire, extremely eager to drink blood.
With diverse forms and faces, bearing various disguises and bodies, / surrounded thus by them, the goddess granting fearlessness to the gods,
"Fear not, O gods, may it be well with you!" While she was speaking, / Ruru the Dānava arrived with a fourfold army.
The seeker of the path of the gods, seeing that excellent blue mountain, / and seeing the army in front of the gods distraught by the goddess,
those Daityas arrived shouting, "Stand, stand!" / Then a dreadful battle commenced between them.
Of the Daityas whose bodies were split by iron arrows crawling on the ground, / slithering like serpents broken by sticks in their fury;
their hearts split by spears, their chests crushed by maces, / their heads severed by axes, their skulls crushed by pestles,
their bellies pierced by the tips of tridents, their necks cut off by excellent swords, / the infantry, together with their struck horses, chariots, and elephants, fell in battle.
All the Daityas reached the battlefield, except Ruru. / Then, seeing his force destroyed, Ruru resorted to illusion.
The goddesses and the gods were bewildered by it on the battlefield. / Through the tāmasic illusion of the goddess, everything became blind darkness.
Then the goddess struck that Daitya with a great javelin; / and struck by it in battle, the darkness of the Daitya vanished.
When the tāmasic illusion was destroyed, the Dānava Ruru / quickly entered Pātāla. There too the supreme goddess,
together with the goddesses, stood enraged facing him. / And as Ruru, lord of the Dānavas, went terrified before her,
having severed his head with the tip of her fingernail and seized his hide, she swiftly / flew up from Pātāla and returned to Mount Puṣkara.
With a great host of maidens, multiform and radiant, / she was seen by the astonished gods carrying the hide and head of Ruru.
The supreme goddess seated herself at her own place of asceticism. / Then the glorious goddesses stood surrounding her.
Undistracted but famished, they begged of that goddess: / "We are hungry, O goddess; grant us excellent food."
Having spoken thus, the goddess then contemplated food for them; / but though she reflected, she could find no great food for them.
Then she meditated upon Mahādeva, Rudra, the omnipresent Paśupati; / and he, the three-eyed Supreme Self, rose from meditation.
Rudra said to that goddess: "What is the matter you wish to speak of? / Speak, O goddess Mahāmāyā, what is on your mind!"
Śivadūtī said: / "O God, within the goat you dwell in the form of a goat; / these [goddesses] will respectfully devour you as their desired food.
You ought to give something here for their nourishment, O Lord of gods; / these mighty ones, desiring food, will impale me on a spike.
Otherwise, famished as they are, they may even devour me by force. / Therefore, considering my plight, provide food at once!"
Rudra said: / "O Śivadūtī, I shall relate one incident that occurred in a previous cosmic age: / At Gaṅgādvāra, the sacrifice of Dakṣa was demolished by my retinues.
There, the sacrifice, having become a deer, ran away with great speed. / It was pierced by me with an arrow and drenched in blood.
Then it smelled like a goat, and my name was made by the gods: / 'You indeed smell like a goat.' But I shall grant another food.
Hear from me, O goddess, one food suitable for them as told by me, / O woman of beautiful hips, O Kālarātri of great splendor!
Whatever pregnant woman, O ruler of gods, wears the garment of another woman, / or touches it, especially that of a man,
that shall be the share, O woman of beautiful hips, of some on the surface of the earth. / Seizing by force even a one-year-old child there,
let them remain well-pleased, devouring it even for many hundreds of years. / Others, when unhonored, should seize their opportunity in the birthing chamber.
They shall dwell thus, O ruler of gods, as destroyers of newborn infants / in the house, in the field, by the pool, and in wells and gardens.
And entering the bodies of those women who constantly weep excessively, / some shall obtain satisfaction."
Śivadūtī said: / "Vile is what has been given by you, afflicting creatures! / You do not understand how to give, O Śaṅkara, especially with relish.
That which is shameful and torments creatures / is not fit to be given as food to them, O Śaṅkara."
Rudra said: / "Formerly in Avantī, when Skanda was blessed by me, / when the tonsure rite of Kumāra took place, O auspicious lady,
the mothers, arriving, prepared an unprecedented feast; / from heaven the hosts of gods came to eat with the mothers.
Formerly, in their house, Brahmā and the other best of gods, / Gandharvas, Apsarases, and all the Yakṣas and Guhyakas,
mountains such as Meru, rivers such as the Gaṅgā, / all Nāgas, elephants, Siddhas, birds, and destroyers of asuras,
Ḍākinīs with Vetālas, surrounded by all the planetary spirits then— / what need of saying more, O goddess, whatever was created by Brahmā here—
all that was given as food, but the food desired by themselves did not reach them." / Śivadūtī said: / "Grant them prepared food that is rare even in heaven,
smeared with oil, with jaggery, delightful, well-cooked, / which has never been eaten elsewhere by another, unprecedented, O supreme lord!"
Thus addressed, the god of gods, Maheśvara, / spoke to them for the sake of food in the presence of Pārvatī:
"Food was prepared by me, made in many ways; / all of that has been exhausted, and nothing else is seen here.
Now that you have arrived, tell me what I should give: / something unprecedented for you that I should especially grant,
untasted by anyone else, I shall give as food: / in the lower part of my navel, these two round, fruit-like,
hanging testicles of mine—eat them together! / And by this food there will be supreme satisfaction."
Having obtained the great favor, all those goddesses bowed down to Śiva / and stood there, and Śarva spoke this word:
"Those men who will perform the auspicious rites without mockery— / their wealth, cattle, sons, wives, house, and so forth,
shall be granted by me, as well as whatever else is in their mind. / Through mockery, they will become long-toothed and poor.
Therefore, censure and mockery should not be made by one who understands. / You shall be known as the Mothers in this world.
Those men who will perform the Kaumudī festival with offerings / of chickpeas, pūrikās, and cakes along with testicle-shaped breads,
with relatives and their own folk, their lineage will never be broken. / The childless shall obtain a son, and one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
handsome, fortunate, enjoying pleasures, skilled in all sciences, / he is exalted in the world of Brahmā in a chariot yoked with swans.
O Śivadūtī, thus was nourishment granted by me to them. / Why did you call me 'shameful'? Hear that now:
Be victorious, O goddess Cāmuṇḍā! Be victorious, O remover of evil spirits! / Be victorious, O all-pervading goddess! O Kālarātri, salutations to you!
O you who possess universal forms, pure one, deformed-eyed, three-eyed one! / O terrible-formed, auspicious one, wisdom, Mahāmāyā, large-bellied one!"
O conqueror of the mind, O fortress of the mind, O terrible-eyed one, O destroyer of agitation, / O Mahāmārī of varied limbs, O lover of song and dance, O auspicious one!
O Vikarālī, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā, O remover of sin, / O you holding a noose in hand, holding a staff in hand, holding dread in hand, O terrifying one!
O Cāmuṇḍā, O you with a flaming mouth, sharp-fanged and mighty, / O goddess fond of jackal mounts, seated upon a corpse, O Śivā!
O terrible-eyed, O fearsome goddess, O cause of terror to all beings, / O Karālī and Vikarālā, O Mahākālī, O Karālinī!
O Kālikarālavikrāntā, O Kālarātri, praise be to you! / O goddess bearing all weapons, praise be to you who are saluted by gods!
Praised in this way by Rudra, the Supreme Lord, / the supreme goddess, Śivadūtī, was pleased and spoke these words:
“Choose a boon, O Lord of the gods, whatever is in your mind.” / Rudra said: / “O goddess, those who praise you with this hymn, O fair-faced one,
be a grantor of boons to them, O goddess, being all-pervading and true. / Whoever ascends this mountain and worships with devotion,
let him be endowed with sons, grandsons, and cattle, and attain prosperity. / And whoever listens with devotion to this hymn of the goddess's origin,
let him, freed from all sins, attain supreme nirvāṇa. / When a king has fallen from his kingdom, restrained and pure on the ninth,
the eighth, and the fourteenth lunar day, fasting, O best of men, / let him regain his kingdom without obstacle within a year.
This power endowed with wisdom is indeed called Śivadūtī. / Whoever constantly hears this with supreme devotion, O king,
freed from all sins, shall attain supreme nirvāṇa. / And whoever recites this with devotion, having bathed in the waters of Puṣkara,
having obtained all this fruit, is exalted in the realm of Brahmā. / In whatever house this written [text] always stays, O king,
there is no dreadful danger of fire or of all kinds of thieves and the like. / And whoever, O wise ones, worships this existing in a book with devotion,
by him the entire threefold world with moving and unmoving beings is worshipped. / Many sons, wealth, grain, and excellent women are born to them,
and jewels, horses, elephants, and servants swiftly accrue to them. / In whatever house this is copied, there too it will surely be so.”

1.32.m: Bhīṣma said: / “By the ripening of what deed does one become a ghost again, / or by what may one be freed here? Tell me that, O highly intelligent one.”
Pulastya said: / “I shall tell you all of this in full, / upon hearing which you shall not fall into delusion again, O best of kings;
by what deed one becomes a ghost, and by what one is freed from this, / [and how one] attains a terrible hell that is hard to cross even for the thirty [gods].
In conversation with good people, and in recounting the sacred pilgrimage sites, / human beings who have fallen into ghostly states are indeed freed.
Indeed, it is heard that formerly, O Bhīṣma, there was a brāhmaṇa of strict vows, / named Pṛthu, renowned everywhere and always established in contentment.
Devoted to Vedic study in his home, ever in yoga, a knower of yoga, / he would spend his time engaged in the method of muttered prayer and sacrifice.
Engaged in forgiveness and compassion, and endowed with forbearance, a knower of reality, / with his mind intent on non-violence, he was established likewise in gentleness.
Endowed with celibacy, possessed of the yoga of asceticism, / he was engaged in rites for the ancestors and engaged in Vedic rites.
Possessed of fear of the next world, dedicated to truthful speech, / dedicated to pleasant words, and dedicated to the worship of guests,
Devoted to sacrifices and charitable works, engaged in abandoning pairs of opposites, / devoted to the rites of his own duty, engaged in the duties of Vedic study,
As he was thus performing deeds with the desire to overcome worldly existence, / many years passed for that virtuous brāhmaṇa in his house.
This thought arose in him concerning visiting holy pilgrimage sites: / ‘With the holy waters of pilgrimage sites I shall bathe this body.’
Restrained, having bathed at Puṣkara at the rising of the sun, / having performed his prayers and salutations, he set out upon the path.
Ahead, he saw five extremely terrifying men / in a forest filled with thorny trees, desolate, devoid of birds.
Seeing them of deformed appearance, most terrible, and sinful to behold, / with his heart somewhat alarmed, he stood motionless.
Then, gathering courage and casting fear far away, / speaking sweetly, he asked: ‘Who are you, deformed? Whence [are you]?
Or what deed was done by which you have attained deformity? / Why have all of you, being of such a kind, set out, and on what path?’
The ghosts said: / ‘Constantly filled with hunger and thirst, overwhelmed by great misery, / all of us are bereft of understanding, unconscious, and confused.
We do not know any direction or intermediate direction, / nor the atmosphere, nor the earth, nor do we know heaven.
This misery that has been described might itself be happiness. / Morning shines forth here at the sight of the rising sun.
I am named Paryuṣita, and the other is Sūcīmukha; / Śīghraga, Rohaka, and the fifth is Lekhaka.’
The brāhmaṇa said: / ‘Whence comes the existence of names for ghosts born from deeds? / Referring to what cause are you endowed with names?’
The ghosts said: / ‘I would always eat delicious food and give stale food to a twice-born; / taking this as the cause, my name is Paryuṣita.
