Many brāhmaṇas desirous of cooked food and the like were pointed out [spitefully] by this one; / referring to this cause, he is considered named Sūcīmukha.
I went away swiftly when begged by a hungry brāhmaṇa; / referring to this cause, O best of the twice-born, [I am] Śīghraga.
On the roof of the house he always eats delicious food out of fear of the twice-born; / there, with an agitated mind, on that account he is recalled as Rohaka.
And always established in silence, when begged, he would scratch the earth; / most sinful among us, by name he is named Lekhaka.
With difficulty Lekhaka moves, while Rohaka has his head downwards; / Śīghraga has attained lameness, and the needle-like one became Sūcīmukha.
Paryuṣita is called long-necked and large-bellied; / with large testicles and hanging lips he was born from this sin.
All this of our own conduct together with the cause has been related to you. / Ask if you have faith, and being questioned we will speak.’
The brāhmaṇa said: / ‘All living beings that abide on the earth are rooted in food; / I wish to hear truly of your food as well.’
The ghosts said: / ‘Hear about our food, despised by all living beings, / hearing which you will censure it again and again, O brāhmaṇa, constantly.
With phlegm, urine, feces, and the dirt from women's limbs, / in houses where purity is abandoned, the ghosts indeed eat there.
In [houses] ruined by women, scattered, where leftover food is thrown about, / and disgusting with filth, the ghosts indeed eat there.
In those devoid of conscience and shame, and those devoid of burnt offerings, / and those devoid of vows, the ghosts indeed eat there.
Where teachers are not worshipped, in houses dominated by women, / and in those seized by anger and greed, the ghosts indeed eat there.
Shame arises in me, dear one, when our food is being described; / and beyond this, nothing else can even be spoken.’
"We ask you about the cessation of the state of a ghost, O you of firm vows! / Tell me that, O ascetic, so that one does not become a ghost."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "By the one-night, two-night, and other penances, by the Cāndrāyaṇa and so forth, / and by other observances performed regularly, a person is not born a ghost.
Whoever day by day serves the three fires, or five, or even one, / full of compassion for living beings, that person is not born a ghost.
Equal in honor and dishonor, equal towards gold and a clod of earth, / equal towards enemy and friend—such a person is not born a ghost.
Constantly devoted to the worship of gods and guests, and to the worship of elders, / and indeed devoted to the rites for the ancestors, a person is not born a ghost.
When a fourth day of the bright fortnight falls on a Tuesday, / one who performs the ancestral offering on it with faith is not born a ghost.
He who has conquered anger and reflection, who is free from thirst and attachment, / forgiving and of a generous nature—such a person is not born a ghost.
And whoever bows down to cows, brāhmaṇas, sacred bathing-places, mountains, rivers, / and indeed to the deities, that person is not born a ghost."
The ghosts said: / "We have heard of various dharmas; now, afflicted, we ask, O sage: / tell us, O wise one, by what deeds one indeed becomes a ghost."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "Especially by eating the food of a śūdra: / if a brāhmaṇa dies while it is still in his belly, he certainly becomes a ghost.
He who abandons mother, father, brothers, sister, and son / when no fault is seen in them—that person is born a ghost.
By officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and by abandoning those fit to sacrifice, / and devoted to the service of a śūdra, that person is born a ghost.
A stealer of deposits, a betrayer of friends, one always fond of cooking for śūdras, / a destroyer of trust, a deceitful man—such a person is born a ghost.
A killer of a brāhmaṇa, a cow-slayer, a thief, a drinker of liquor, a violator of the guru's bed, / and a stealer of land or a maiden—such a person is born a ghost.
Having obtained a shared sacrificial fee, he hides it away alone; / devoted to atheistic thoughts, he indeed is born a ghost."
While the foremost brāhmaṇa was speaking thus, a sound of kettledrums resounded in the sky, / and a shower of flowers fell upon the earth, released by the thousands by the gods.
Celestial chariots arrived on all sides for the ghosts, / on account of conversation with this brāhmaṇa and the recitation of what is meritorious.
"Therefore, with every effort, converse with the virtuous, / if you are concerned with your highest good, O son of Gaṅgā, without sloth.
The mark of all dharma is this story of the five ghosts; / whoever recites it a hundred thousand times—in his family no man is born a ghost.
Or if one hears it constantly, endowed with supreme faith / or filled with devotion, that person is not born a ghost."
Bhīṣma said: / "For what reason is Puṣkara praised in the sky / by sages endowed with dharma? And how is it attained here?
By whom it is attained, how it was attained, and how, once attained, it bears fruit— / tell me all that, as I ask purely out of curiosity."
Pulastya said: / "Ten million ṛṣis residing in the southern lands arrived / for the purpose of bathing at Puṣkara, O king, but Puṣkara had gone into the sky.
Reflecting on that, all those sages, devoted to breath-control, / meditating on the supreme Brahman, remained for twelve years.
Brahmā, the great ṛṣis, and the gods headed by Indra gathered there; / the ṛṣis, having disappeared from sight, spoke of their very difficult vows:
'Let the invocation of Puṣkara be performed with a mantra, O twice-born! / Through the three Ṛg-verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā", it will become present.
And through the chanting of the Aghamarṣaṇa, it will become fruit-yielding.' / At the end of the speech, all those brāhmaṇas did exactly so.
By what they performed and by the command, those twice-born attained purity; / those brāhmaṇas from the south and the north were censured in the dharmaśāstras,
as well as others from the mountains, not worthy of an invitation to an ancestral rite. / For this reason, O king, it remained thus in the sky.
On the full-moon day of Kārttika, Puṣkara attains purification through bathing, / accompanied by Brahmā, O king, granting merit to all.
Whichever castes come there, they all become vessels of merit, / equal to the twice-born without a doubt, [even] without the mantra, O king.
When the asterism belonging to Agni occurs on that full-moon day of Kārttika, / that lunar day is to be known as great, supreme for bathing and gift-giving.
When the asterism belonging to Yama occurs on that lunar day, / that lunar day is also declared by ascetics to be of great merit.
When the asterism sacred to Prajāpati occurs on that lunar day, O ruler of men, / that is called Mahākārttikī, rare even for the gods.
And when it falls on Sunday, Thursday, or Monday—indeed on these three days of the week— / these three asterisms have been proclaimed by Brahmā himself.
Here, the merit of a horse sacrifice certainly accrues to one who has bathed; / a gift becomes imperishable, and likewise the water libation to the ancestors.
When the sun is in the Viśākhās and the moon is in the Kṛttikās, / that conjunction is named Puṣkara, exceedingly rare at Puṣkara.
When the auspicious sacred place of the Grandfather descends from the sky, / those who bathe there will attain exalted worlds.
They will have no desire for other merit, whether performed or unperformed, / O great king; this is spoken as the truth.
It is recited here as the foremost sacred place among sacred places on earth; / no sacred place more meritorious than this is recited in the worlds, O king.
Especially on the full-moon day of Kārttika, it is auspicious, purifying, and sin-removing; / and the Sarasvatī came forth from that forest of Udumbara trees.
By her that sacred place of Puṣkara, frequented by sages, was filled. / In the south, not far away, shines the peak of the mountain,
resembling a heap of dark collyrium, blue with grassy turf in color; / by her that peak stands as if it were Puṣkara situated in the sky,
resembling a dense mass of clouds rising up, filling the sky in the rainy season, / rich with the fragrance of kadamba flowers, adorned with kuṭaja and arjuna trees,
standing as if to ascend the path of the chariot of the sun, / like the breasts of women, rounded, thrill-swollen, and smooth.
The peak shines with delightful bilva fruits on all sides, / embellished all around with swarms of humming bees,
lovely with the calls of cuckoos, resplendent with the calls of peacocks. / On that enchanting peak arose the most charming,
auspicious river, endowed with holy waters, the daughter of Brahmā; / very broad, she issued from a cluster of bamboos, flowing toward the north.
Having gone not very far from there, she again turns her course away; / from then on, that goddess remained gracious and visible.
Abandoning concealment out of compassion for living beings, / [she became] Kanakā, Suprabhā, Nandā, and the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī.
She was declared by Brahmā as five-streamed at the Puṣkara sacred places. / On her banks are very delightful sacred places and temples,
frequented on all sides by sages and by perfected beings as well; / among all of them, the Sarasvatī will be the cause of dharma.
The giving of gold, land, and cows at those sacred places brings great elevation; / given by men who have bathed, it produces an imperishable fruit.
The foremost sages proclaim the giving of grain to be supreme, and likewise the giving of sesame; / whatever was given by men at those sacred places is designated as supreme, the cause of dharma."
Whichever woman or man, restrained and with effort, observes fasting unto death there, / or fixes their mind on that sacred ford, enjoys at will the fruit in Brahmā's abode.
Those motionless and moving beings who die in its vicinity due to the exhaustion of their karma / all easily obtain the entire fruit of sacrifice, which is otherwise difficult to attain.

Therefore, she is the fire-drill producing the fruit of dharma for those whose minds are tormented by sorrows such as birth; / with all one's being, this great river Sarasvatī, yielding lovely fruits, should be diligently frequented by men.
Those men who continually drink her pure water there / are not mere humans; they are gods abiding here on earth.
The fruit that is attained by twice-born men through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, / is attained here by Śūdras, by their very nature, through merely bathing.
Even those who are great sinners, merely by seeing Puṣkara, / are freed from their sins and go to heaven upon the dissolution of the body.
The fruit that belongs to the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice is obtained by a man / who fasts there at Puṣkara, quickly and with little exertion.
He who in the month of Māgha gives sesame seeds to a good twice-born man / according to his means and with devotion, shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever man undertakes fasting, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow there, / he too shall attain heaven at the end of his body.
Even those belonging to classes of thieves who dwell in its vicinity / go to heaven by its power, without any doubt.
Furthermore, those men engaged in the occupation of Śūdras who fast for three nights / and bestow wealth upon twice-born men, endowed with the power of Brahman,
when dead, ascend a celestial vehicle, seated on a lotus, four-armed, / and attain companionship with Brahmā, without returning to rebirth.
[Now hear of] the confluence of the Gaṅgā, where the Gaṅgā arrived to see the best of rivers, / the Sarasvatī, which had emerged from the sky for the sake of peace.
Having gone there, the pure water of the Sarasvatī, frequented by gods and Siddhas, / spotless, and venerated by the hosts of Vidyādharas,
was drunk in the measure of a handful by him by whom the highest was attained. / Looking toward the eastern quarter, [Sarasvatī] said: 'O friend Gaṅgā, by you
I am left alone, separated [from you]; where shall I go, bereft of kin?' / Knowing her to be thus weeping, emaciated by grief,
the Gaṅgā came from the eastern country to see her who was dejected in mind; / and seeing that illustrious, afflicted [river], embracing her,
and wiping her eyes, the Gaṅgā then spoke these words: / 'Do not weep, O illustrious one! A difficult deed was performed by you, my friend,
namely the purpose of the gods, which indeed could never have been done by another. / Therefore, O illustrious one, the gods have come to see you;
worship should be offered to them by action of speech, mind, and body.' / Sarasvatī, having performed the ritual sequence of worship to the chiefs of the gods,
gradually, the daughter of Brahmā then met with her group of friends. / Between the eldest and the middle [Puṣkara] is that confluence, renowned in the world.
The daughter of Brahmā faces west, but the Jāhnavī faces north. / Then all those gods who had arrived at Puṣkara,
recognizing her difficult deed, sang a hymn of praise to her: / 'You are discernment, you are intellect, you are Lakṣmī, you are learning, you are the supreme path;
you are faith, you are the highest steadfastness, wisdom, intelligence, delight, forbearance; / you are accomplishment, you are svadhā and svāhā, you are deemed the great purifier;
you are twilight, night, luster, prosperity, wisdom, faith, Sarasvatī; / you are the sacrificial knowledge, the great knowledge, and the auspicious esoteric knowledge;
you are logic, economic livelihood, and what is called the science of governance. / Salutations to you of holy water! Salutations to you who flow to the ocean!
Salutations to you, the deliverer from sins! Salutations, O goddess, dear to the world!' / Having thus been praised by those divine beings intent on their own purpose,
that goddess Sarasvatī stood there, facing east— / the goddess consisting of all sacred fords, accompanied by all the immortals.
She is to be known by the wise as Prācī, and so is the declaration of Brahmā. / There the sacred ford named Śuddhāvaṭa, sacred to Brahmā, is remembered.
Even those who are great sinners, merely by seeing it, / purified, enjoy the pleasures of celestial beings near Brahmā.
Those best of men who observe fasting unto death there, / when dead, go to heaven free from fear in a celestial vehicle of Brahmā.
Even a small gift given there by them to those who know Brahman / is as if given by those purified souls for a hundred future births.
Those men who carry out repairs on broken and cracked [structures] there, / having reached the world of Brahmā, rejoice, ever happy.
Whatever worship, silent recitation, and fire oblation is performed here by embodied beings, / all that fruit is endless for those devoted to the worship of Brahmā.
Through the offering of a lamp there, one acquires the eye of knowledge transcending the senses; / through the offering of incense, one attains the abode frequented by Brahmā.
Or what is the use of speaking much? Whatever is given at the confluence / is declared to bear endless fruit, whether for the living or for the deceased;
from bathing, silent recitation, and fire oblations, it brings about endless fruit. / Rāma indeed came there and offered the funeral ball for Daśaratha,
and performed the ancestral rite there at the place shown by Mārkaṇḍeya. / There is a square stepped-well there; those men who offer funeral balls there,
all go to heaven in a celestial vehicle yoked with swans. / At that stepped-well, Brahmā indeed performed the funeral sacrifice,
a sacrifice with excellent sacrificial fees completed, being the best of sacrifice-knowers. / The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers,
and the Ādityas are designated as their great-grandfathers. / Having summoned all three groups, Viriñci spoke again:
'You should always receive the offering of funeral balls and the rest, abiding here; / and whatever ancestral duty is performed here shall bear endless fruit.'
For their sustenance, their fathers and grandfathers are gratified; / through the libation of water they obtain satisfaction, and through the offering of funeral balls, heaven.
Therefore, setting aside everything, one should offer funeral balls at Prācīna; / having given them with effort, a son should satisfy all the ancestors.
Established in front of Lord Prācīneśvara, / it is called the Primordial Ford, granting liberation merely upon being seen.
Having merely touched the water there, one is freed from the bondage of birth; / by bathing, one becomes an eternal attendant of Brahmā.
Having bathed at the Primordial Ford, whatever man offers food with concentrated mind, / even a little, shall generally attain heaven.
Whatever man, having bathed there, gives wealth to those devoted to Brahmā, / even with dish of rice and lentils or with gold, rejoices happy in heaven.
When the Prācī Sarasvatī is present there, what higher thing can men seek? / From bathing in her comes fruit yielding satisfaction, marked by austerities, sacrifices, and the like.
Those men who drink the holy, eastern goddess Sarasvatī / are not to be known as men, but as gods—so declared sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having reached the river Sarasvatī, there is no restriction regarding bathing anywhere— / whether having eaten or not eaten, by day or at night.
That ancient ford is remembered as the most excellent of all fords; / it is celebrated as destroying sin and generating religious merit for living beings.
Moreover, those purified souls who, having bathed there, / worship Janārdana according to their capacity, go to heaven.
Viṣṇu is foremost among the gods; where Sarasvatī was honored by him, / that is the supreme sacred ford on earth: so said the son of Brahmā.
Therefore, regarding that great sacred ford as bringing great fortune, / looking out for the Mandākinī, Sarasvatī remained there.
Svāyambhuva declared that sacred ford to be supreme among all sacred fords, / where a holy junction is obtained together with the Mandākinī.
Remaining in that place, goddess Sarasvatī was praised by the gods; / seeing her alone, with a dejected face and a depressed mind,
Brahmā then created a female companion endowed with beauty, with pure eyes. / Hari also quickly produced Hariṇī, lotus-eyed.
The lord of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt, also created Vajriṇī. / The god Nīlakaṇṭha, whose emblem is a bull, with the grace of a fine deer,
The three-eyed god produced a companion for Sarasvatī. / Looked upon by her companions, O king, she was a celestial beauty.
delighted, began to flow by the command of the gods, the great river; / then, together with her companions, she set out to flow eastward.
Sarasvatī is remembered as the very best among all of them. / Whichever deer on earth drink the water of the eastern Sarasvatī—
they too will go to heaven, just like the best of the twice-born through sacrifices. / Here this eastern Sarasvatī is to be known as like a wishing-jewel;
likewise, this great river has become the source of desired fruit. / Looking toward the southern quarter, she turned her face westward again.
Thus was she addressed by Gaṅgā: 'Go to the eastern direction; / and do not forget me, O goddess; go as you have arrived.'
